utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hurko. Please be seated. Mr. Hurko, you'll first be examined by Ms. Hochhauser. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Hochhauser, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, good morning, or good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber, are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And where is it that you live now?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hurko, you have given -- you gave a statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not uncommon to start with the first question whether the witness would state his full name and date of birth, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: My name is Sefik Hurko. I was born on the 22nd of November, 1957, in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hurko, in -- on 24 January 1999, you gave a statement to the ICTY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And prior to that, on 16 November of 1994, you gave a statement to local authorities in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, on the 1st of September, 2011, did you have the opportunity to review an amalgamation of those two previous statements into one document?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to please put 65 ter number 28362 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise -- I see we're looking at the first page. Do you recognise the signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the last page of the document. I apologise. The page before. So it would be page 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I do recognise it. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have an opportunity to review over this past weekend and yesterday a copy of this statement in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And is it correct that yesterday you noticed two additional changes that you wanted to make. One being that in paragraph 41, the third sentence should read 10 July -- "10 June" where it now reads "10 July"?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 42, where it reads -- where the first sentence begins, "A couple of days after that," that the "that" should be changed to "on 9 July."

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, on the 2nd of September, did you make a number of other observations and changes that you would like to make or small corrections that you would like to make to the statement?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could ask, please, for 65 ter number 28371 to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is, just for reference, this is the information report that I was just referencing. I believe it's up in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it. And it looks very much the same as what we received in hard copy a minute ago. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Great. And I see also that the B/C/S version of it is there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And I'm going to refer you now to the information in paragraph 2 on page 1 of this document in which it indicates certain changes that you would like to make to your statement. Does what's written here on the monitor in front of you accurately reflect the other changes that you would like to make to your statement?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, what was shown in the English is more than what was shown in B/C/S. Therefore, I take it that you would like to ask the witness about the beginning of page 2 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at all of the points on page 1 and 2 that are indicated with -- with letters before them alphabetically.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you had an opportunity to review just before -- just before entering the courtroom, the summary that's listed under the bullet point 3, which begins, I believe, on the second page in the B/C/S version and goes through the third page. And, on the English, it's contained only on the second page.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, I had a look at this a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And does this accurately summarise the additional information that you provided?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, in regard to both 28362, which was the previous statement, the ICTY amalgamated statement that you looked at, the 2 -- and -- and 28371, the changes that are now reflected on the monitor in front of you and the additional information provided, if you had the opportunity today to provide the same information, would you answer the questions the same today as you did then?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration before this Chamber, can you affirm that together 28371 and 28362, as well as the two date corrections that we previously talked about, contain a truthful and accurate account of the -- of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter number 28362 along with associated exhibits 08506 and 08880 into evidence. I would note for the Chamber there is an additional document that's listed which is an associated exhibit, that's with the 65 ter number 09316, but on further consideration of that document it's not being offered because the -- the document itself doesn't add anything to the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None. Madam Registrar, could you please assign numbers. First, the statement given by the witness, the amalgamated statement of 2011 I think it was.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28362 becomes Exhibit P164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Next one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 08506 becomes Exhibit P165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. Next one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 08880 becomes Exhibit P166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And document 09316 becomes Exhibit P167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecution indicated that they would not tender that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what is missing, apparently, is the information report which has 65 ter number 28371 and was uploaded a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. And I also would like to offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is -- number P167 is now vacated. Then document 28371 becomes Exhibit P167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P167, it being the information report dated 2nd of September, 2012, is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the Court's permission I will now summarise the witness's written evidence as contained in the ICTY amalgamated statement which was originally our intention to offer pursuant to 92 ter. I intend to still lead additional evidence on the additional information live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it being admitted, it should not duplicate what is found there. Please read your summary for the public, and I take it that you have explained to the witness what purpose it serves.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. It's been explained to the witness that what I say is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: On 14 August 1992, Mr. Hurko was detained in the town of Madjar by Serb soldiers along with his -- he was detained along with his mother, his father, and his uncle. Mr. Hurko and his father were questioned about Rajko Kusic of the Rogatica Crisis Staff and were severely beaten during that questioning. His uncle is believed to have been killed. Mr. Hurko and his parents were then brought by Kusic to the detention centre at the Rogatica secondary school along with other Muslim men, women, and children. On 15 August, 1992, Mr. Hurko was brought to a cross-roads in the direction of the village of Kosovo, where he observed a mini-bus coming from the direction of Rogatica which was carrying civilians. Shortly thereafter he heard firing, and the Serbs that accompanied the bus returned to where he was and boasted that they had killed all the Balijas. The next day Mr. Hurko was brought to Rasadnik camp and he made the connection from what he saw and heard there that the men in the bus who had been killed were those taken from Rasadnik the morning before. Mr. Hurko was imprisoned at Rasadnik camp from 16 August 1992 until he was transferred to Kula prison on 30 April of 1994. During the 20 months that he was imprisoned at Rasadnik, Mr. Hurko and his father were severely beaten, and he both witnessed and heard about the routine beating and killing of numerous other Muslim detainees. Female detainees at Rasadnik were taken out in the middle of the night, forced to perform sexual acts with elderly male prisoners, and were also raped. Prisoners of both genders were subject to numerous sexual humiliations and abuses. Throughout his detention Mr. Hurko and the other detainees were forced to do labour, including going to the front lines and recovering the bodies of Serb soldiers from minefields. Mr. Hurko's statement provides evidence of individual perpetrators of these crimes as well as who was running these crimes. On 5 October, 1994, after a total of approximately 26 months in captivity, Mr. Hurko was exchanged. And that concludes the summary, Your Honours. So if I may inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, as you know, this Court has already carefully read your statement which is now in evidence, so I'm going to ask you several questions with the hope to either clarify the information in the statement or add additional information, okay? And you have to --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if we could please have Exhibit P164, the amalgamated statement, back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 24 of your statement, after you describe being brought to Rasadnik on the 16th, it reads: "I asked Mujo Jasarevic whether were there any other prisoners in the camp. He said there were but they had been taken in a mini-bus that day to collect hay." Can you tell us what bay is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I was taken to Rasadnik on the 16th, from the secondary school to Rasadnik on the 16th. When Mujo told me on that day, he was referring to the 15th when I, too, was in the village of Kosovo. So it was the previous day. That is the day that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going ask you -- and I'm guilty of the same thing, but if you could slow down a little bit, please. You were detained at Rasadnik camp from 16 August 1992 to 30 April 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, approximately how many people were detained in the camp at various times during the period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: When I arrived in the camp, when I arrived in Rasadnik camp, there were about 45 people there and the people who had came from the secondary school. So there were about 100 people there. Some were sent away for exchanges; others would arrive; and there were about 100 women, children, elderly people, men who were fit for military service. These people were present in the camp during the period that I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that the -- the number -- the actual numbers fluctuated during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the ethnicities of these people were?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the age range of the people that were there?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: From 6 to 75 or 80 years old. One woman even gave birth in the prison. So there were new-born children and people who were 75 or 80 years old. Nezirja [phoen] Dizdarevic was the name of the woman who gave birth in Rasadnik camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what the conditions were in the camp in terms of food and shelter and medical provisions?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: When I arrived in the camp where the men were, there were only certain facilities to the side and nothing else. There were three tin cans in a corner. I asked Mujo Jasarevic what sort of tin cans they were. He said we used them as a toilet. And in another corner there was these suitcases. I asked him about them. He said there were some other inmates, 25 to 30 of them, and they went to collect hay, but I realised that those were the people who were killed from the previous day. And there was nothing else in the room where we spent our time lying down, apart from those planks that I have mentioned. We slept on those planks. Food would arrive. It wasn't very good. It was pretty bad. And it wasn't much. One dish consisted of perhaps 200 grams of food and we had a slice of bread, and this would be provided to us in the morning and in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And were there -- were there separate areas for the men and the women?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, there were separate areas for men and women, but there was no door, so everything could be seen. And there was only one entrance, and then there were two separate rooms, one for the men, one for the women, but the door was open. In fact, there was no door, so it was all open.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And the women and children and elderly that you've told us were there, were there -- were they treated differently? Were their conditions any different than the men of military age?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: No. The conditions were the same for everyone. There were no medical supplies, no medicine. I didn't notice that they were provided with protection of any particular kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like -- I'm going to turn, please, to paragraph 25 of your statement, and it says there: "From 16 August 1992 to 1 September 1992, I went to work and nobody beat me." Can you describe, please, for the Chamber what work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: When I arrived in the prison, I didn't go anywhere for a day or two. Later a mini-bus arrived and said, You're going to work. The mini-bus took us to the main centre in Rogatica, to the main street, and we swept that street. Mostly we took Muslim things out from their houses and loaded them onto lorries. The items were then taken to Serbian houses or flats and we would unload them. There were two mosques that were razed to the ground, and we also cleared through those mosques during that period of time in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: When you say you took Muslim things out of the houses, how did you know that they were Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Well, since I lived in Rogatica, and there was this place called Rudo as well, I knew that these houses were Muslims. I knew that that was the case before the war, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "things"? What kind of things?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I mean stoves, furniture, sofas, dressing tables, fridges. They took all those items out. The rooms were left empty. And sometimes they'd take water too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, were you ever given any choice about whether to do this or any other kind of labour that you did during your detention?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any choice. We did everything we were ordered to do. We had to do everything. The worst sort of things that they didn't want to the do. They forced us to perform such labour, which we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if you can tell us what were the repercussions of refusal? Or did anyone ever try to refuse?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone who dared to refuse to comply, and if anyone had refused to comply with the orders, that person would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraphs 25 through 27 of your statement, you describe beatings of both you and your father on a particular occasion. Can you briefly give the Chamber, tell them with a little more specificity what you mean when you say "we were beaten"? What happened?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I was beaten on several occasions. My father and I were beaten on several occasions. Around the 1st of September, 1992, Miso Vojinovic was the warden of the prison and his assistant was Despot, that was his surname, and his nickname was Buco. About 2.00 in the morning they took my father out and he was detained for about half an hour. I could hear him banging on something. Half an hour later, Despot or Buco came to fetch me and asked me to stand up. When I got into the room, I saw Miso Vojinovic and Buco. They took a baton, Buco was standing in front of me. He said he was interested in some sort of trenches in a place called Sarani and he was interested in mines. I started saying that I had never been there, that I hadn't dug the trenches there. He then started beating me with that baton. I don't know how many times he hit me. I could just see that my shirt was tight. They later asked me about weapons and whether I had a rifle or something like that, and then he took a larger baton, and when he started hitting me with that larger baton I fell to the ground. When I fell, they took a bucket of water and threw the water over me. Then they told me to stand up, I stood up, and they took me back to the prison where my father was. When I saw my father, my father asked me whether I had been beaten. I said, Yes. I asked him whether he had been beaten. He said, Yes. In the morning when they had a look at my back it was all swollen, and that was also the case for my father. So that was one occasion that I can describe for you. If you need me to describe other occasions, I can. And then on the following morning some inspector called Djida arrived, and he spoke to my father outside about 9.00 in the morning and they took him to the police station in Rogatica. I went to work but I couldn't work there. I remained standing. There were two policemen, one of home was called Pero Rajak arrived. The other's surname was Kovacevic. They told me I should go to the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Kovacevic then --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you there for a moment. Just going back to what you were telling us about that beating that you gave as an example. You've described one -- that one incident. How -- can you tell us, did you see other prisoners -- other detainees subject to the same types of treatment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, in addition to that, could I ask you to speak a bit more slowly so that the interpreters and transcribers are able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, did you see other prisoners treated to -- subject to the same kind of treatment that you've described now for the Court in terms of beatings?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I saw them killing someone. I would hear them beating people. I knew that similar things were taking place and even worse things. After the 28th of July, 1993, there were certain things that I heard and saw. It wasn't just what happened to me and my father.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: When you say there were certain things that you heard and saw, are you referring to the treatment of the -- the similar treatment of other people in the camp detained with you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you ever hear during any of these beatings any language, ethnic or otherwise, language directed at the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you please describe that for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Which incident are you interested in? There were several incidents. Could you please specify the one you are interested in? When they killed Becir Cutaj on the 21st of March, 1993, we were working in a place called Trnovo. It's a village in the vicinity of Rogatica. We were digging trenches. About 1700 hours we returned to the camp, and Adena Musevic [phoen] gave us some macaroni for dinner and a slice of bread. There was a dish by the side and someone asked whose dinner that was, and some said it was Becir Cutaj's dinner and that Vinko had taken him to his office, so no one touched the dish. We went to the room that we slept in. We spent about two hours there, and then you could hear some groaning in Vinko's room. Some crying. You could hear some banging, someone being beaten. This took about half an hour -- this lasted for half an hour or an hour and then there was a break for an hour and then it would continue, and that evening Becir Cutaj didn't appear. On the following morning Vinko Bojic said that Suljo Kustura should remain behind. He to do something. He remained behind. Becir had been killed that evening, and Suljo buried him. He told us that he took him out in a sort of wheel barrow and he had been cut into pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm specifically asking about is whether in -- in your memory of any of incidents that you observed of beatings or killings whether you heard -- whether there was a specific type of language coming from the people who were doing the beating or killing directed at the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Well, they were cursing Balija mothers, Balijas, Ustashas, where is Alija for you? Who did you vote for? That's what they said everyday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to draw your attention, now, to approximately 1st of April 1994. And can you tell us on or around that date where you were brought and -- where you began -- where you were brought, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Exactly on the 1st of April, three military trucks came in front of the camp. They said that all who are capable of working should go on these trucks. We were there, and also from other Sartorovici [phoen], Torni Do [phoen], Osevo [phoen], other villages, there were other men and everybody boarded these three trucks and we went towards Ustiprace. About 4 or 5 kilometres away, they told to us get out. When we got out, we walked for about half a kilometre and then was a large number of Serb soldiers there. There were heavy weapons like mortars of different calibres. Also there were howitzers. Now I'm not very knowledgeable about this kind of thing. So they lined us up there and they said to us an offensive against Gorazde has been launched. Now you are going to be working here. You will have an assignment to carry ammunition and food there, and you should do all of this for the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: We were supposed to carry all of that towards a hill called Trovrh.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us approximately how long did you do that work for?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I worked until the 17th or 18th. I carried ammunition and food everyday, and I saw -- I took a dead soldier from there, and about ten times I carried wounded people too. After the 17th, the 18th, we had a break for about two or three days, and then one morning, a truck came, and they said that ten or fifteen Muslim camp inmates were supposed to get on that truck. They drove us towards Ustiprace, but before that there was this placed called Mesic. That's where the truck went and we went through some woods, some mountain called Gnjila. The road was a macadam road. As we were driving across this Gnjila we got to this other side of the Trovrh hill, and you could see Gorazde from there as well. It was about --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Can I ask you was this a different place that you were brought to during the previous weeks of that month?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Before we went to Mesici. That's a different place.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And could you please tell the Court on the day that you were brought to this different place --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, actually, if I can ask for Exhibit 167 to be placed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: That day, did there come -- did there come a point when somebody told you to speed up because General Mladic was coming?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes. But I haven't gotten to that yet. Yes, well, that did happen but I'll tell you about that later. When they brought us to behind this hill Trovrh we saw Gorazde, and they said that we should work in this forest and that we should cut some logs and place them across some kind of hole and apparently some tanks were supposed to go that way. Then Vinko Bojic, the person who brought us there, said, Speed up a bit because General Mladic is supposed to come here. And then we got a bit confused. We started working a bit faster, and within three or four minutes a group of soldiers showed up together with Mladic. These soldiers walked up to him to say hello.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you describe, first of all, when -- when General Mladic walked up, you said with a group of soldiers, can you tell us how they were -- how he was dressed and how the soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Well, they all wore camouflage uniforms and they also had some kind of insignia, whatever. I'm not knowledgeable about this kind of thing. What a general wears, whatever. I mean, I didn't even dare look properly. But they all wore camouflage uniforms and they pridely said -- proudly said hello to him because the general had come. And they said hello and the Muslims had left the trenches over those days, and now whether he saw something there, whether he didn't see anything, he said, You see, America is feeding them, America is providing them with clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Again, I have to ask you to slow down -- slow down in your answers. Who said, "America is feeding them, America is providing them with clothing"?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, you said you heard other soldiers addressing him. How were they addressing him?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, what was it -- and if you can, just answer -- as I go through these questions, just try to answer the questions specifically. What was it -- what, if anything, did you hear General Mladic say toward you or about you and your group?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: He congratulated the soldiers on their victory, and then when he got a bit closer he said to Vinko, Who are these guys working? Because we were wearing civilian. And he said we were inmates from Rogatica. And he asked whether we were loyal or whether we had been captured, and Vinko said loyal. And then he said, Let them go out a bit here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Who said are they -- are they loyal or are they captured?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object as to that being speculation unless there's some foundation for this witness being asked to testify as to the intent of the speaker of those words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the only question was asked from the witness how he understood that. Whether that's right or wrong and whether that accurately reflects the intention of the speakers is a matter still to be seen, but the witness may answer the question. How did you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just go on now. He said that we should get out and then we lined up, one next to another, and he asked Vinko whether we were loyal, whether we were loyal to the Serb republic or whether we had been captured at the front line. And Vinko said that we had not been captured but that we were loyal. Then he made a sign with his hand towards Gorazde, saying, See this Gorazde here, in a day or two it's going to be in Serb hands. You who wish to remain here will have to be baptised, and those who do not want to do that will be transferred to Alija's state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- could you take care that Mr. Mladic's voice is -- that he is speaking at low level of volume. Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And did he say anything after that.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: He said that we should go to work and then he disappeared. I mean, I don't know when he left with these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you can tell us -- are you able to just tell the Chamber where exactly was this that you saw him? Where did this event take place?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: It's below Trovrh. I mean, I don't know the villages around Gorazde. I don't know their names. There were 5 or 6 kilometres away from Gorazde, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And is Trovrh a hill in that area?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes. From Rogatica and from my village you can see it from this side, that hill I mean, and -- I mean, from both sides. I mean, from Rogatica and Gorazde you can see this hill, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Hochhauser, the interpreters request that we switch off all microphones when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I apologise for failing to do it, Your Honour. In any case, that concludes the Prosecution's questioning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the Prosecution's questions for it witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Ivetic. If we take a break now for 20 minutes we would have 50 minutes left for -- after the break. Could you give us -- already give an indication as to how much time you think you would need. It is, of course, a 92 ter witness which is different from a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I had already sent an e-mail to my colleague on the other side that an hour and 40 minutes was estimated for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take the break first, and we'll resume at 25 minutes -- no, let me see. We'll resume at 1.30. But could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to the Court taking a break, something just happened in the Court. Rather than myself characterise what happened, could I ask the Chamber to review the tape -- the camera that's focussed on Mr. Mladic during proceedings. It happened at the last ten seconds of the -- when we all stood up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll ask to be provided with a copy of the last minutes of what happened in court. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom again. Meanwhile, the Chamber reviewed the tape. Mr. Mladic, you made gestures at the end of last session which are inappropriate, which you shouldn't have made. Waving with your finger, et cetera. You should refrain from doing that. Let that be clear. It is inappropriate behaviour. At the same time, the Chamber, having considered it, saw no reason at this moment under the present circumstances to take any measures in relation to that behaviour. But let it be clear: Again, you should refrain from any gestures which expresses agreement or disagreement with what witnesses say. Under all circumstances, you should not do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Hurko. The break took more time than expected. Apologies for that. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. Today I have a set of questions --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic is counsel for Mr. Mladic and he is the one who will cross-examine you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, today I have a set of questions that I need to ask you to try and better understand the testimony that you have given, both in the witness statement and in court. I would ask that you pay attention to precisely what it is I'm asking you so that your answers can be focussed on that question, and I promise that I will try to go through this as easily as possible with you. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, first, I want to clarify some background matters as to yourself. Could you tell us about your educational background; specifically, what school you finished and when?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I finished a school for catering in 1980, 1979. Whatever. I don't know the exact year. I am a trained cook.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. And I apologise. I was just waiting for the translation into English and the transcript to catch up with us. If I can move along then. Am I correct that you served a period of compulsory military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes. In the quartermaster's corps. I was a cook there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly where and when it was that you completed your compulsory military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: In 1976, in Nis, Leskovac, and Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now you've mentioned already that you were in the quartermaster's corps. Was that your only assignment or was there another unit speciality or branch of the JNA that formed a part of your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: At first I had this infantry training and this gun. The rifle M-48. It's the only thing I knew about. That's all. And then this quartermaster's work. I learned that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you remember who were -- or was your commanding officer for the -- both of the stint in the infantry and the stint in the quartermaster corps?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: There was this second lieutenant. I really cannot remember the name. It's been such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'll move along. Sir, am I correct that you, upon your discharge -- upon discharging your duty with the JNA, that you had to register with the local defence office to have your official duty station assigned in the event of war or mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you were registered? That is to say, which Office of National Defence were you registered in?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: In Rogatica where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your official war-time assignment or duty station as per your registration in the Rogatica local national defence office?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I was on the reserve police force but I worked on the ground, and I hardly ever came for these lineups and whatever because I worked elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that as part of this registration you had an automatic obligation to report for duty to your appointed duty station or war-time assignment in the case of a war or a call-up?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, if I worked in north Yemen, if I was out there, I couldn't come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the transcribers and interpreters ask you to take a break. You see "[Previous translation continued] ..." when you start your question already. Please keep that in mind and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours. And I apologise to both the transcribers and the translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can move forward to the years 1991 and 1992, am I correct that the JNA at that time began calling up citizens to be mobilised for the events that were taking place on the territory of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I worked in north Yemen at the time, in 1991. I came back, and I don't remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time receive a call-up summons asking you to report for duty from the JNA in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that in 1992 you were working as a cook for RO Bosna Putovi, Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At that time were you still residing in Rogatica or were you residing in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I lived in Rogatica with my wife and children, in the Rudo neighbourhood. I came to Rogatica every week --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear where the witness worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at your statement in paragraph 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, have you noticed the observation by the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you to repeat for us where it is that you worked in regard to the last answer, as the interpreters did not hear. The only part that has been recorded is that you lived in Rogatica with your wife and children in the Rudo neighbourhood and you came to Rogatica every week. They missed where you were working. Could you please complete the record of your last answer.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I worked in Sarajevo, but I lived in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, am I correct that we're going till 2.15 today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then it's time to stop. That is, of course, due to the fact that it took a while to review the video. Mr. Hurko, we'll adjourn for the day, and I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is your testimony as you have given it today or whether it is your testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 5th of September, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of September, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.15 p.m.,
